TAB:96:4/r12.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:96:4/r12.speaker: عطاء بن يسار
TAB:96:4/r12.claim: ʿAta ibn Yasar says Iqra was the first surah revealed from the Qur'an.
TAB:96:4/r12.anchor: عن عطاء بن يسار ،   قال :  أوّل سورة نزلت من القرآن اقْرأْ باسْمِ رَبّكَ

TAB:96:4/r13.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:96:4/r13.speaker: مجاهد
TAB:96:4/r13.claim: Mujahid says Iqra was the first Qur'anic revelation; one transmission adds that Nun and the Pen followed.
TAB:96:4/r13.anchor: عن مجاهد ،   قال :  أوّل ما نزل من القرآن :  اقْرأْ باسْمِ رَبّكَ وزاد ابن مهديّ :  ن والْقَلَمِ

TAB-FULL:v24p527#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p527#2/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p527#2/r2.claim: Qatāda calls the pen a great blessing from God, without which life could not be sustained or set right.
TAB-FULL:v24p527#2/r2.anchor: عن قتادة، {اقرأ باسم ربك الذي خلق} [العلق: 1] قرأ حتى بلغ {علم بالقلم} [العلق: 4] قال: " القلم: نعمة من الله عظيمة، لولا ذلك لم يقم

TABATABAI:96:1-7/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:96:1-7/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:96:1-7/r10.claim: The ba is causal: God taught reading or writing, with the pen serving as the means; the clause may be circumstantial or a fresh statement.
TABATABAI:96:1-7/r10.anchor: الباء للسببية أي علم القراءة أو الكتابة والقراءة بواسطة القلم

ZAJJAJ:v5p345/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p345/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p345/r2.claim: God taught writing with the pen.

TABRISI:96:3-10/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:96:3-10/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:96:3-10/r4.claim: God taught the scribe to write, taught people expression through the pen, or taught writing by means of the pen; writing benefits religion and worldly life.
TABRISI:96:3-10/r4.anchor: علم الكاتب أن يكتب بالقلم أو علم الإنسان البيان بالقلم أو علم الكتابة بالقلم

TABRISI:96:3-10/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:96:3-10/r5.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:96:3-10/r5.claim: The pen is a tremendous blessing from God: without it religion would not stand and life would not improve.
TABRISI:96:3-10/r5.anchor: القلم نعمة من الله عظيمة لولاه لم يقم دين ولم يصلح عيش

TABRISI:96:3-10/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:96:3-10/r6.speaker: بعضهم
TABRISI:96:3-10/r6.claim: An unattributed poem describes the pen's ink as venomous serpents' saliva and the gathered honey of hands, praising its striking material effect.
TABRISI:96:3-10/r6.anchor: لعاب الأفاعي القاتلات لعابه وأري الجنى اشتارته أيد عواسل

TABRISI:96:3-10/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:96:3-10/r7.speaker: كعب
TABRISI:96:3-10/r7.claim: A report says Adam was the first to write.
TABRISI:96:3-10/r7.anchor: وقيل أراد سبحانه آدم لأنه أول من كتب عن كعب

TABRISI:96:3-10/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:96:3-10/r8.speaker: الضحاك
TABRISI:96:3-10/r8.claim: A report says Idris was the first to write.
TABRISI:96:3-10/r8.anchor: أول من كتب إدريس عن الضحاك

TABRISI:96:3-10/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:96:3-10/r9.speaker: قيل
TABRISI:96:3-10/r9.claim: The verse may refer to every prophet who wrote with a pen, since God alone taught each of them to write.
TABRISI:96:3-10/r9.anchor: أراد كل نبي كتب بالقلم لأنه ما علمه إلا بتعليم الله إياه

THALABI:v10p244/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p244/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p244/r8.claim: “Who taught by the pen” means teaching writing and script.
THALABI:v10p244/r8.anchor: الذي علم بالقلم يعني الخط والكتاب

THALABI:v10p244/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p244/r9.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v10p244/r9.claim: Asked whether he should write down what he hears from the Prophet, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr is told yes, because God taught by the pen.
THALABI:v10p244/r9.anchor: قلت: يا نبي الله أكتب ما أسمع منك من الحديث؟ قال: «نعم، فاكتب فإن الله علم بالقلم

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170/r1.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170/r1.claim: God taught writing or the written book by means of the pen; Muqātil gives the same gloss.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170/r1.anchor: قوله {الذي علم بالقلم} قال الكلبي (¬1)، ومقاتل (¬2): علم الكتاب بالقلم.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170/r2.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170/r2.claim: God taught human beings to write with the pen.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170/r2.anchor: (قال أبو إسحاق: أي علم الإنسان الكتابة بالقلم (¬3).)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170#4/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170#4/r1.speaker: صاحب النظم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170#4/r1.claim: The object of “taught by the pen” is omitted and supplied by verse 5: God taught humans through the pen what they did not know; repeating “taught” emphasizes it.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170#4/r1.anchor: وقال صاحب النظم: مفعول قوله: {علم بالقلم} محذوف، فلما ذكر قوله: {علم الإنسان ما لم يعلم} انتظم

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170#4/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170#4/r2.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170#4/r2.claim: Al-Kalbī likewise understands the knowledge in verse 5 as writing in a book by means of the pen.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p170#4/r2.anchor: وهذا معنى قول الكلبي؛ (لأنه قال) (¬8): {علم الإنسان ما لم يعلم} من الكتاب بالقلم.

WAHIDI-QT:96:4/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:96:4/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:96:4/r1.claim: God taught by the pen, explaining His teaching as handwriting and writing.
WAHIDI-QT:96:4/r1.anchor: { الذي علم بالقلم } ثم بين ما علم فقال { علم الإنسان ما لم يعلم } وهو الخط والكتابة

WAHIDI-QT:96:5/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:96:5/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:96:5/r1.claim: The knowledge God taught humanity includes handwriting and writing.
WAHIDI-QT:96:5/r1.anchor: { الذي علم بالقلم } ثم بين ما علم فقال { علم الإنسان ما لم يعلم } وهو الخط والكتابة

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:96:1-8/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:96:1-8/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:96:1-8/r5.claim: Teaching by the pen is teaching writing.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:96:1-8/r5.anchor: الذي علم بالقلم } ثم بين ما علم، فقال:

ELMALILI:96:1-8#2/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:96:1-8#2/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:96:1-8#2/r15.claim: God teaches by the pen and writing, the instrument by which knowledge is learned; humans made from a clinging thing would otherwise know neither pen nor script.
ELMALILI:96:1-8#2/r15.anchor: O kalem ile tâlim eden de kalem ile yazıyı öğreten, o vâsıta ile ilim belleten de O’dur

ELMALILI:96:1-8#2/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:96:1-8#2/r17.speaker: Beyzâvî
ELMALILI:96:1-8#2/r17.claim: Beyzawi says God recounts the human's beginning and end while moving him from the lowest state to the highest, first indicating rational knowledge of God and then signifying transmitted knowledge.
ELMALILI:96:1-8#2/r17.anchor: Beyzâvî der ki: “Allah sübhânehu insanı ehass-ı merâtibden

ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r1.claim: Creation rationally points to knowledge of God, while recitation and writing transmit what the reader and writer received; the Qur'an includes rational proofs but chiefly signifies through its heard wording that the Prophet learned from God.
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r1.anchor: Doğrudan doğru hilkati mütalaanın ma‘rifetullâha delâleti aklîdir. Kıraat ve kitabette ise okuyan ve yazandan nakil haysiyeti ile delâlet-i sem‘iye vardır

ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r2.claim: It is significant that the first revealed verses unite rational and transmitted proof and present recitation, writing, and knowledge as great divine gifts; the pen also encourages the community to literacy.

ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r3.claim: The Prophet needed no writing to recite, while his unlettered reading establishes prophethood and the Qur'an's divine origin; 29:48 states this explicitly.
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r3.anchor: Peygamber’in kıraat için yazıya ihtiyâcı olmadığı iş‘âr olunmakla beraber şüphe yok ki kalem ile tâlimin de büyük bir ikrâm-ı rabbânî olduğu beyan buyurulmuş

ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r4.claim: The Prophet never wrote with his own hand and needed no writing to retain revelation because God promised he would not forget in 87:6; he recited and dictated the revelation to scribes for the community.
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r4.anchor: hıfz u zabt için de yazmaya ihtiyâcı olmadığı, fakat nâzil olanı ümmetin hıfzı için vahiy kâtiblerine okuyup yazdırdığı mâlumdur.

ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r5.claim: The common view is that the Prophet did not learn to read others' writing; at Hudaybiyya, he famously asked Ali which word to erase.
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r5.anchor: Nitekim Hudeybiye musâlahanâmesinde yazılan bir kelimeyi silmek için hangisi olduğunu Hazret-i Ali’ye sorduğu mâruftur.

ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r6.claim: Some accounts in al-Shifa and related works say the Prophet instructed his scribe Muawiya how to prepare the pen and beautify the basmala, suggesting knowledge of writing.
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r6.anchor: Şifâ ve etrafında mezkur olduğu üzere sonradan kâtibi Hazret-i Muaviye’ye أَلق الدَّوَاةَ وَحَرِّفِ الْقَلَمَ وَطَوِّلِ الْبَاءَ

ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r7.claim: Elmalılı says such instructions may have come through special revelation and that learning writing during the twenty-three prophetic years is plausible, without compromising the miracle of becoming a reader while unlettered.
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r7.anchor: sene Kur’ân’ı okumak ve yazdırmak vazifesi olmuş olan Hazret-i Peygamber’in bu müddet zarfında yazıyı da bellemiş olması müsteb‘ad değil, mâkuldür.

ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r8.claim: The Prophet's not writing or reading books before prophethood would support the claim in 29:48; after prophethood, learning script would confirm rather than undermine it, though he certainly wrote nothing himself or studied other books.
ELMALILI:96:1-8#3/r8.anchor: Fakat bilfiil yazmadığı ve başka kitap mütalaa etmediği muhakkaktır

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:96:1/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:96:1/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:96:1/r1.claim: These were the first revelation; the command to read addresses Muhammad and all Muslims, and its repetition stresses the importance of reading and knowledge, through which humans are distinguished among living things.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:96:1/r1.anchor: İlk vahyin “oku” emriyle başlaması ve bu emrin iki defa tekrar edilmesi

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:96:1/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:96:1/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:96:1/r7.claim: The pen preserves and transmits sciences, wisdom, history, books, and revelation across generations; its functional sense includes all tools of reading, writing, and information exchange through computers.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:96:1/r7.anchor: bilinen kalemden bilgisayara kadar bütün okuma, yazma ve bilgi alıp verme araçlarını kapsadığını

CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r1.claim: Qalam is borrowed from Ethiopic and ultimately derives from Greek kalamos; the repeated ʿallama resembles the repeated word in 106:1–2.
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r1.anchor: Qalam ist aus dem Äthiopischen entlehnt und geht letztlich auf gr. kalamos zurück

CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r3.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r3.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r3.claim: ʿAllama bi-l-qalam can mean teaching with a pen or teaching writing; the variant reading that explicitly says writing is likely a later clarification.
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r3.anchor: ʿAllama bi-l-qalam kann entweder „mit dem Schreibrohr belehren“ oder „das Schreibrohr (= das Schreiben) lehren“ bedeuten

CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r7.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r7.speaker: Neuwirth
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r7.claim: Neuwirth emphatically interprets qalam as a heavenly pen describing the Preserved Tablet, used by heavenly scribes; the author allows this possibility but considers human writing plausible too.
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r7.anchor: Neuwirth vertritt sehr dezidiert diese Interpretation

CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r8.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r8.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r8.claim: Later plural uses of qalam refer to earthly pens or lots, supporting the possibility that the verse concerns human writing and the reliable transmission of revelation.
CORPUSCORANICUM:96:4-5:anmerkung/r8.anchor: alle übrigen (allerdings deutlich späteren) Verwendungen des Wortes qalam, die im Plural ʾaqlām stehen

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p387/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p387/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p387/r1.claim: Earlier prophets’ teachings were transmitted orally, and the present Torah is a written record of tradition whose divine and narrator wording cannot be distinguished; the Qur’an was preserved word for word under God’s scrutiny.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p387/r1.anchor: for the Qur’ ān the Almighty made elaborate arrangements that all of it be composed of His words

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p387/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p387/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p387/r2.claim: Written preservation of revelation was unprecedented and especially a favor to unlettered Arabs, who thereby preserved guidance intended for all mankind.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p387/r2.anchor: since the Arabs were unlettered they were not fully aware of the use of the pen

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r7.claim: Writing preserves sciences, wisdom, earlier reports, statements, and revealed books; without it religious and worldly affairs could not be ordered.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r7.anchor: وما دونت العلوم، ولا قيدت الحكم، ولا ضبطت أخبار الأولين ولا مقالاتهم ولا كتب الله المنزلة إلا بالكتابة

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r8.claim: An unnamed poet compares writing pens to swift, dark serpents and describes their progress as if white blades played through them.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r8.anchor: ورواقم رقش كمثل أراقم ... قطف الخطا نيالة أقصى المدى

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r10.claim: The two objects of ʿallama are omitted because the passage's purpose is to attribute teaching to God.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r10.anchor: ومفعولا علم محذوفان، إذ المقصود إسناد التعليم إلى الله تعالى

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r11.speaker: ابن الزبير
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r11.claim: A reading attributed to Ibn al-Zubayr inserts “who taught writing by the pen”; the author treats it as explanatory gloss, not Qur'an, because it differs from the codex consonantal text.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r11.anchor: وقدر بعضهم الذي علم الخط، بالقلم: وهي قراءة تعزى لابن الزبير، وهي عندي على سبيل التفسير

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r12.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r12.claim: The apparent teacher is everyone who writes with a pen; other views identify Idris or Adam, the first to write.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p507/r12.anchor: والظاهر أن المعلم كل من كتب بالقلم. وقال الضحاك: إدريس، وقيل: آدم لأنه أول من كتب

ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#3/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#3/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#3/r1.claim: God taught people through the pen and writing, and can teach the Prophet without that means; karam is giving what is fitting without ulterior motive, and in its absolute intensive form it is uniquely God's attribute.
ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#3/r1.anchor: الذي علم بالقلم أي علم ما علم بواسطة القلم لا غيره تعالى

ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#3/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#3/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#3/r2.claim: An alternative treats the second Read as not emphasis but as a lead-in to remove the Prophet's excuse, making Your Lord is most generous a circumstantial clause about the command's subject.
ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#3/r2.anchor: وجوز أن لا يكون اقرأ هذا تأكيدا للأول وإنما ذكر ليوصل به ما يزيح العذر

ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#4/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#4/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#4/r8.claim: The passage praises writing’s benefits and high status: without it religion would not stand and life would not be sound; the pen and script alone suffice as a sign of God’s subtle wisdom.
ALUSI-FULL:v30p180#4/r8.anchor: وقد أدمج سبحانه وتعالى التنبيه على فضل علم الكتابة لما فيه من المنافع العظيمة ونيل الرتب الفخيمة

ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r1.claim: Writing was ancient among non-Arab peoples but a later arrival among Arabs, especially in the Hijaz, according to the apparent historical reports.
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r1.anchor: وظاهر الآثار أن الكتابة في الأمم غير العرب قديمة وفيهم حادثة لا سيما في أهل الحجاز

ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r2.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r2.claim: The continuation of a pen poem uses an image of a jinn and eager hands around the writing tool to evoke the power of writing.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r3.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r3.claim: Another poem that al-Zamakhshari attributes to an unnamed poet praises calligraphic pens and the far reach of writing.
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r3.anchor: ومما نسبه الزمخشري في ذلك لبعضهم وعنى على ما قيل نفسه ورواقم رقش كمثل أراقم

ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r4.speaker: الكلبي، الهيثم بن عدي
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r4.claim: Al-Kalbi and al-Haytham ibn Adi report that writing was ancient among non-Arabs but newly acquired in the Hijaz, transferred from Hira by Harb ibn Umayya after he learned it in the region of al-Anbar; the chain of reported teachers leads through Aslam ibn Sidra to Maramir ibn Murra.
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r4.anchor: وأنهم أخذوا من أهل الأنبار وذكر الكلبي والهيثم بن عدي أن الناقل للخط العربي من العراق إلى الحجاز حرب ابن أمية

ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r5.claim: Himyar reportedly used the separate, unjoined Musnad script, taught only with permission; one claim counts twelve major script families, which al-Alusi allows only if these are origins since derivative scripts are too many to count.
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r5.anchor: وكان لها شأن عندهم فلا يتعاطاها إلا من إذن له تعلمها وأصناف الكتابة كثيرة

ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r6.claim: Some scholars object to calling people most generous in correspondence, even though they regard it as modest praise for rulers, and criticize applying it to Jews or Christians; people should show reverence and gratitude for the generosity of their Lord.
ALUSI-FULL:v30p181/r6.anchor: ولم ير بعض العلماء من الأدب وصف غيره تعالى كما يفعله كثير من الناس في رسائلهم

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p474#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p474#2/r1.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p474#2/r1.claim: Most commentators say this was the first sura revealed and that its first five verses, through the words about what humanity did not know, were the first revelation.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p474#2/r1.anchor: أكثر المفسرين: على أن هذه السورة أول سورة نزلت من القرآن، وأول ما نزل خمس آيات من أولها

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p479#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p479#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p479#2/r1.claim: The pen means handwriting and writing.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p479#2/r1.anchor: الذي علم بالقلم} يعني الخط والكتابة

BAYDAWI-FULL:96:4-8/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:96:4-8/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:96:4-8/r1.claim: God taught writing with the pen, which preserves knowledge and conveys it to distant people; a reading explicitly adds the word “writing.”
BAYDAWI-FULL:96:4-8/r1.anchor: أي الخط بالقلم، وقد قرىء به لتقيد به العلوم

BAYDAWI-FULL:96:4-8/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:96:4-8/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:96:4-8/r3.claim: God recounts humanity's beginning and destination to show the favor of raising it from the lowest rank to the highest, affirm His lordship and generosity, and move from rational proof to sensory evidence.
BAYDAWI-FULL:96:4-8/r3.anchor: وقد عدد سبحانه وتعالى مبدأ أمر الإنسان ومنتهاه إظهارا لما أنعم عليه

BAYDAWI-FULL:96:18-19/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:96:18-19/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAYDAWI-FULL:96:18-19/r4.claim: A report promises the reciter a reward as though he had recited the entire set of shorter suras.
BAYDAWI-FULL:96:18-19/r4.anchor: من قرأ سورة العلق أعطي من الأجر كأنما قرأ المفصل كله

BINTSHATI:v2p13/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p13/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p13/r2.claim: She presents the surah’s opening as the first revelation, noting that Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari report no disagreement about that account.
BINTSHATI:v2p13/r2.anchor: والمشهور كذلك أنه أمل سورة نزلت من الوحي. ولم يشر "ابن إسحاق" في (السيرة النبوية) إلي خلاف

BINTSHATI:v2p13/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p13/r3.speaker: عائشة أم المؤمنين
BINTSHATI:v2p13/r3.claim: Aisha recounts Muhammad’s true dreams, retreat to Hira, Gabriel’s command and three embraces, and the recitation of the opening five verses, which remained fixed in his heart; no grading is stated.
BINTSHATI:v2p13/r3.anchor: عن "السيدة عائشة أم المؤمنين" قالت: "كان أول ما ابتدئ به رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - من الوحي

BINTSHATI:v2p13/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p13/r4.speaker: عائشة أم المؤمنين
BINTSHATI:v2p13/r4.claim: Aisha continues that Muhammad saw Gabriel in the sky, returned to Khadija, and was reassured because his character included kinship, truthfulness, trustworthiness, hospitality, and helping in adversity; no grading is stated.
BINTSHATI:v2p13/r4.anchor: فقالت: أبشر يا ابن عم واثبت، فوالله لا يخزيك الله أبداً، إنك لتصل الرحم وتصدق الحديث

BINTSHATI:v2p14/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p14/r3.speaker: الفخر الرازي
BINTSHATI:v2p14/r3.claim: Al-Razi also transmits that only al-Alaq’s first five verses came at the start; the remainder came after public opposition and were joined to the surah by God’s command.
BINTSHATI:v2p14/r3.anchor: أن الذي نزل من السورة أول الوحي، آياتها الخمس الأولى

BINTSHATI:v2p14/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p14/r4.speaker: أبو حيان
BINTSHATI:v2p14/r4.claim: Al-Bahr al-Muhit says the surah is Meccan and its opening was the first revelation at Hira, as established in Bukhari and elsewhere; it judges the claims that al-Muddaththir or the Fatiha came first unsound.
BINTSHATI:v2p14/r4.anchor: وقول جابر: أول ما نزل المدثر، وقول أبي ميسرة عمرو بن شرحبيل: أول ما نزل الفاتحة، لا يصح

BINTSHATI:v2p15/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p15/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p15/r1.claim: The reports in al-Tabari and the Prophetic biography stop the first-revelation account at verse five, supporting the view that the opening alone was first revealed.
BINTSHATI:v2p15/r1.anchor: حيث يقف الحديث فيهما عن اول ما نزل من الوحي، عند الآية الخامسة

BINTSHATI:v2p22/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r2.claim: Knowledge is apprehending a thing as it truly is, and its opposite is ignorance; she had surveyed Quranic uses of knowledge in her commentary on al-Takathur.
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r2.anchor: العلم إدراك الشيء على حقيقته، ونقيضه الجهل

BINTSHATI:v2p22/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r3.claim: The pen is the instrument of writing, as in the opening oath of Surat al-Qalam.
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r3.anchor: والقلك أداة الكتابة، ومنه آية القلم: {ن وَالْقَلَمِ وَمَا يَسْطُرُونَ}

BINTSHATI:v2p22/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r4.speaker: الطبري
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r4.claim: Al-Tabari interprets teaching by the pen as teaching humans writing they had not known.
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r4.anchor: علم الإنسان الخط بالقلم ولم يكن يعلمه

BINTSHATI:v2p22/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhshari likewise takes it as writing, which records sciences, wisdom, ancient reports, and revealed books, enabling religion and worldly life to function; Abu Hayyan quotes him.
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r5.anchor: وما دونت العلوم ولا قيدت الحكم ولا ضبطت أخبار الأولين ومقالاتهم

BINTSHATI:v2p22/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r6.speaker: الفخر الرازي
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r6.claim: Al-Razi discusses the honor of the pen and the wisdom in its creation; Ibn Qayyim devotes a chapter to the pen’s rank and benefits.
BINTSHATI:v2p22/r6.anchor: ما ذكره الفخر الرازي في شرف القلم وحكمة خلقه

BINTSHATI:v2p23/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r1.claim: Continuing the preceding discussion of Ibn Qayyim, the author lists his twelve pens, from the primordial decree and revelation through juristic, medical, political, accounting, judicial, testimonial, dream, historical, linguistic, and polemical writing.
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r1.anchor: أولها: وأعلاها وأجلها قدراً قلم القدر السابق الذي كتب الله به مقادير الخلائق

BINTSHATI:v2p23/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r2.speaker: الفخر الرازي
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r2.claim: Al-Razi reads a symbolic sequence: creation from a clot signals rational proofs of divine power and wisdom, while writing by the pen signals revealed evidence, law, and prophethood.
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r2.anchor: فكأنها إشارة إلى معرفة الربوبية، والتعليم بالقلم إشارة إلى النبوة

BINTSHATI:v2p23/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r3.speaker: النيسابوري
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r3.claim: Al-Nishaburi offers an interpretation like al-Razi’s symbolic contrast between rational evidence and knowledge of revelation.

BINTSHATI:v2p23/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r4.claim: She sets aside symbolic readings and takes the pen as the writing tool that records, preserves, and transmits knowledge across time, place, and generations.
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r4.anchor: وحيث لا مجال للإشاريات في منهجنا، نطمئن إلى أن الآية لفتت إلى سر القلم

BINTSHATI:v2p23/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r5.claim: The Quran draws an unlettered Prophet and people’s attention to the pen as a Creator’s sign and to acquired knowledge as a human distinction; revelation connects knowledge with Adam’s honor and stewardship.
BINTSHATI:v2p23/r5.anchor: بما تعني من اختصاص الإنسان دون سائر الكائنات بالقلم وكسب العلم

BINTSHATI:v2p24/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p24/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
BINTSHATI:v2p24/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to gloss the verse as teaching writing by the pen; Abu Hayyan judges this to be an explanatory reading.
BINTSHATI:v2p24/r3.anchor: ما روى عن "ابن عباس" من أنه قرأ الآية: "علم الخط بالقلم"

BIQAI-FULL:v8p482/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p482/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p482/r1.claim: Writing has benefits beyond comprehension and supports the ordering of worldly and religious life, in this life and the next, displaying God's subtle wisdom and governance.
BIQAI-FULL:v8p482/r1.anchor: لأنها انبنت عليها استقامة أمور الدنيا والدين في الدنيا والآخرة

DURR-FULL:v8p560/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p560/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v8p560/r1.claim: The author classifies the chapter as Meccan and counts nineteen verses.

DURR-FULL:v8p560/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p560/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p560/r6.claim: Aisha's account describes true dreams and retreat at Hira before Gabriel commands him to read, presses him three times, and recites the first five verses; Muhammad returns trembling to Khadija.
DURR-FULL:v8p560/r6.anchor: عن عائشة أم المؤمنين أنها قالت: أول ما بدئ به رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من الوحي الرؤيا الصالحة في النوم

DURR-FULL:v8p563/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p563/r3.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p563/r3.claim: He calls the pen a great blessing: without it religion would not stand and life would not be sound.
DURR-FULL:v8p563/r3.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {الذي علم بالقلم} قال: القلم نعمة من الله عظيمة لولا القلم لم يقم دين

RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r1.claim: A phrase beginning with bi-l-qalam is incomplete without an elided verb, such as كتبْتُ بالقلم; similarly, بالله in an oath implies أحلف, and على اسم الله when permitting travel implies travel in God’s name.
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r1.anchor: اتفقوا على أنه لا بد فيه من إضمار فعل فإنك إذا قلت بالقلم لم يكن ذلك كلاما مفيدا

RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r2.claim: Omitting the implied verb is more eloquent because stating one verb would confine the phrase to that act, while omission lets the hearer infer that all needs depend on refuge in or beginning with God’s name; he compares this with saying الله أكبر without specifying a comparison.
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r2.anchor: الحذف في هذا المقام أفصح والسبب فيه أنه لو وقع التصريح بذلك المضمر لاختص قوله أعوذ بالله بذلك الحكم المعين

RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r3.speaker: سيبويه
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r3.claim: Sībawayh says this bāʾ can only govern kasra, which is why it is kasra; the simile kāf also governs kasra but is itself fatḥa because it stands in for a noun and is weak, whereas a particle exists through its effect and is strong.
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r3.anchor: قال سيبويه لم يكن لهذه الباء عمل إلا الكسر فكسرت لهذا السبب

RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r4.claim: The bāʾ may be original, as in the statement that Muhammad was no unprecedented messenger, or extra, with several functions.
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r4.anchor: الباء قد تكون أصلية كقوله تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r5.claim: The bāʾ of adhesion is exemplified by أعوذ بالله and بسم الله.
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r5.anchor: أحدها للإلصاق وهي كقوله { أعوذ بالله } وقوله { بسم الله }

RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r6.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r6.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī holds that the bāʾ may indicate partitive meaning.
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r6.anchor: وثانيها للتبعيض عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه

RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r7.claim: An extra bāʾ can strengthen negation, as in ما ربك بظلام للعبيد.

RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r8.claim: An extra bāʾ can make a verb transitive, as in ذهب الله بنورهم, meaning أذهب نورهم.

RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p86/r9.claim: The bāʾ can mean في; the cited poetic line حل بأعدائك ما حل بي is glossed as حل في أعدائك, and oath-bāʾ is classed under adhesion.

BURHAN:v1p377/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v1p377/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
BURHAN:v1p377/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says Ishmael was the first to establish Arabic writing, though reports on this subject are numerous and conflicting.
BURHAN:v1p377/r1.anchor: وكان ابن عباس يقول أول من وضع الكتاب العربى إسماعيل عليه السلام قال والروايات فى هذا الباب كثيرة ومختلفة

BURHAN:v1p377/r2.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v1p377/r2.speaker: author
BURHAN:v1p377/r2.claim: The author holds that writing was divinely taught, citing God’s teaching by the pen and the Quranic oath by the pen; Adam and other prophets may have been taught it.
BURHAN:v1p377/r2.anchor: والذى نقوله إن الخط توقيفي لقوله ﴿ علم بالقلم علم الإنسان ما لم يعلم ﴾ وقال تعالى ﴿ ن والقلم وما يسطرون ﴾

BURHAN:v1p377/r3.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v1p377/r3.speaker: author
BURHAN:v1p377/r3.claim: Some claim ancient Arabs did not know letter names, grammar, case, or hamza; the author answers that letter names were among what God taught Adam.
BURHAN:v1p377/r3.anchor: وزعم قوم أن العرب العاربة لم تعرف هذه الحروف بأسمائها وانهم لم يعرفوا نحوا ولا إعرابا

BURHAN:v1p377/r4.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v1p377/r4.speaker: author
BURHAN:v1p377/r4.claim: The author accepts that Abu al-Aswad established Arabic grammar and al-Khalil prosody, but says the sciences existed earlier, declined, and were revived by the two imams.
BURHAN:v1p377/r4.anchor: وما اشتهر أن أبا الأسود أول من وضع العربية وأن الخليل أول من وضع العروض فلا ننكره

BURHAN:v1p377/r5.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v1p377/r5.speaker: author
BURHAN:v1p377/r5.claim: Ancient codex spelling distinguishes words with wāw and yāʾ and omits hamza after a quiescent letter; this shows early Muslims knew orthography, and some scholars opposed abandoning codex spelling.
BURHAN:v1p377/r5.anchor: ومن الدليل على عرفان القدماء من الصحابة وغيرهم ذلك كتابتهم المصحف على الذى يعلله النحويون

BURHAN:v1p377/r6.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v1p377/r6.speaker: الفراء
BURHAN:v1p377/r6.claim: Al-Farra says following the codex is preferable when its spelling has a valid basis in Arabic usage.
BURHAN:v1p377/r6.anchor: وأسند إلى الفراء قال اتباع المصحف إذا وجدت له وجها من كلام العرب

BURHAN:v1p377/r7.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v1p377/r7.speaker: مالك
BURHAN:v1p377/r7.claim: Malik says codices must retain the first orthography; al-Dani reports no scholar opposed him. Malik also forbids changing extra written wāw and alif absent from pronunciation, as in أولوا, أولات, and الربوا.
BURHAN:v1p377/r7.anchor: وقال أشهب سئل مالك رحمه الله هل تكتب المصحف على ما أخذته الناس من الهجاء فقال لا إلا على الكتبة الأولى

BURHAN:v4p255/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v4p255/r1.speaker: author
BURHAN:v4p255/r1.claim: The instrumental باء marks the tool of an action, as in writing with a pen; the common analysis also takes باء in بسم الله as instrumental.
BURHAN:v4p255/r1.anchor: وللاستعانة وهي الدالة على آلة الفعل نحو كتبت بالقلم ومنه في أشهر الوجهين ﴿ بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم ﴾

ITQAN:v3p284/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v3p284/r3.speaker: author
ITQAN:v3p284/r3.claim: The opening of “Read” similarly previews the Qur’an: it commands reading, begins in God’s name, signals legal knowledge and the principles of religion, and reports God’s teaching of what humans did not know; it can therefore be called the Qur’an’s title.
ITQAN:v3p284/r3.anchor: وكذلك أول سورة ( اقرأ فإنها مشتملة على نظير ما اشتملت عليه الفاتحة من براعة الاستهلال

ITQAN:v4p442/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p442/r5.speaker: ابن فارس
ITQAN:v4p442/r5.claim: Ibn Faris argues that script was taught by God, citing the verses about the Pen and teaching humanity; these letters belong among the names taught to Adam.
ITQAN:v4p442/r5.anchor: وقال ابن فارس الذي نقوله إن الخط توقيفي لقوله تعالى

ITQAN:v4p363/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r1.speaker: وهب بن منبه
ITQAN:v4p363/r1.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih says Idris was Noah’s grandfather and was called Khanuq, a Syriac name.
ITQAN:v4p363/r1.anchor: وقال وهب بن منبه إدريس جد نوح الذي يقال له خنوخ وهو اسم سرياني

ITQAN:v4p363/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r2.speaker: author
ITQAN:v4p363/r2.claim: An alternative derivation makes the Arabic name Idris come from studying, because he studied the scriptures extensively.
ITQAN:v4p363/r2.anchor: وقيل عربي مشتق من الدراسة لكثرة درسه الصحف

ITQAN:v4p363/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r3.speaker: سمرة
ITQAN:v4p363/r3.claim: A weak al-Mustadrak report from Samura describes Idris and says God raised him to the sixth heaven after seeing earthly injustice; it identifies this with 19:57.
ITQAN:v4p363/r3.anchor: وفي المستدرك بسند واه عن الحسن عن سمرة قال كان نبي الله إدريس أبيض طويلا ضخم البطن عريض الصدر قليل شعر الجسد كثير شعر الرأس

ITQAN:v4p363/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r4.speaker: ابن قتيبة
ITQAN:v4p363/r4.claim: Ibn Qutayba says Idris was raised when he was 350 years old.
ITQAN:v4p363/r4.anchor: وذكر ابن قتيبة أنه رفع وهو ابن ثلاثمائة وخمسين سنة

ITQAN:v4p363/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r5.speaker: ابن حبان
ITQAN:v4p363/r5.claim: Ibn Hibban’s Sahih calls Idris a prophet and messenger and says he was the first to write with a pen.
ITQAN:v4p363/r5.anchor: وفي صحيح ابن حبان أنه كان نبيا رسولا وأنه أول من خط بالقلم

ITQAN:v4p363/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
ITQAN:v4p363/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas says a thousand years separated Noah and Idris.
ITQAN:v4p363/r6.anchor: وفي المستدرك عن ابن عباس قال كان فيما بين نوح وإدريس ألف سنة

ITQAN:v4p363/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r7.speaker: الجواليقي
ITQAN:v4p363/r7.claim: Al-Jawaliqi says Ibrahim is an ancient non-Arabic name, rendered by Arabs in several forms, most commonly Ibrahim.
ITQAN:v4p363/r7.anchor: قال الجواليقي هو اسم قديم ليس بعربي وقد تكلمت به العرب على وجوه أشهرها إبراهيم

ITQAN:v4p363/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r8.speaker: الجواليقي
ITQAN:v4p363/r8.claim: Al-Jawaliqi notes the form Ibraham was read among the seven, alongside forms with a deleted yāʾ and Ibraham without the alif.
ITQAN:v4p363/r8.anchor: وقالوا إبراهام وقرئ به في السبع وإبراهيم بحذف الياء وإبرهم

ITQAN:v4p363/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r9.speaker: author
ITQAN:v4p363/r9.claim: The name Ibrahim is also given a Syriac meaning, merciful father.
ITQAN:v4p363/r9.anchor: وهو اسم سرياني معناه أب رحيم

ITQAN:v4p363/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r10.speaker: الكرماني
ITQAN:v4p363/r10.claim: Al-Kirmani gives another derivation of Ibrahim from barhama, meaning intense looking.
ITQAN:v4p363/r10.anchor: وقيل مشتق من البرهمة وهي شدة النظر حكاه الكرماني في عجائبه

ITQAN:v4p363/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r11.speaker: author
ITQAN:v4p363/r11.claim: The passage gives Abraham’s genealogy as son of Azar, also called Tarah, through Nahor, Sharukh, Raghu, Falikh, Abir, Shalikh, Arfakhshadh, and Shem to Noah.
ITQAN:v4p363/r11.anchor: وهو ابن آزر واسمه تارح بمثناة وراء مفتوحة وآخره حاء مهملة بن ناحور

ITQAN:v4p363/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r12.speaker: الواقدي
ITQAN:v4p363/r12.claim: Al-Waqidi says Abraham was born two thousand years after Adam was created.
ITQAN:v4p363/r12.anchor: قال الواقدي ولد إبراهيم على رأس ألفي سنة من خلق آدم

ITQAN:v4p363/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r13.speaker: أبو هريرة
ITQAN:v4p363/r13.claim: A report in al-Mustadrak from Abu Hurayra says Abraham circumcised himself at 120 and died aged 200.
ITQAN:v4p363/r13.anchor: وفي المستدرك من طريق ابن المسيب عن أبي هريرة قال إختتن إبراهيم بعد عشرين ومائة سنة

ITQAN:v4p363/r14.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r14.speaker: النووي وغيره
ITQAN:v4p363/r14.claim: Al-Nawawi and others report a view that Abraham lived 175 years, differing from the report that he died at 200.
ITQAN:v4p363/r14.anchor: وحكى النووي وغيره قولا أنه عاش مائة وخمسة وسبعين

ITQAN:v4p363/r15.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r15.speaker: الجواليقي
ITQAN:v4p363/r15.claim: Al-Jawaliqi says Ismail’s name is also pronounced with a final nūn.

ITQAN:v4p363/r16.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r16.speaker: النووي وغيره
ITQAN:v4p363/r16.claim: Al-Nawawi and others say Ishmael was Abraham’s eldest son.
ITQAN:v4p363/r16.anchor: قال النووي وغيره هو أكبر ولد إبراهيم

ITQAN:v4p363/r17.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r17.speaker: author
ITQAN:v4p363/r17.claim: Isaac was born fourteen years after Ishmael and lived 180 years.
ITQAN:v4p363/r17.anchor: ولد بعد إسماعيل بأربع عشرة سنة وعاش مائة وثمانين سنة

ITQAN:v4p363/r18.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p363/r18.speaker: أبو علي بن مسكويه
ITQAN:v4p363/r18.claim: Abu Ali ibn Miskawayh says Ishaq means laughing in Hebrew.
ITQAN:v4p363/r18.anchor: وذكر أبو علي بن مسكويه في كتاب نديم الفريد أن معنى إسحاق بالعبرانية الضحاك

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p10/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p10/r1.speaker: عائشة رضي الله عنها
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p10/r1.claim: ʿĀʾisha says revelation began with true dreams and seclusion at Ḥirāʾ; Gabriel's repeated commands to recite introduced al-ʿAlaq, and the shaken Prophet was comforted by Khadīja, who cited his virtues. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim transmit it.
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p10/r1.anchor: عن عائشة رضي الله عنها أنها قالت: "أول ما بدئ به رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - من الوحي الرؤيا الصادقة في النوم

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p11/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p11/r2.speaker: بعض علمائهم
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p11/r2.claim: Ibn Shihāb relays from Muḥammad b. ʿAbbād that some scholars said al-ʿAlaq's first five verses were revealed at Ḥirāʾ; the remainder came later as God willed.
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p11/r2.anchor: أنه سمع بعض علمائهم يقول: كان أول ما أنزل الله على رسوله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - {اقرأ باسم ربك الذي خلق

IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p183/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p183/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p183/r1.claim: God’s oath by the alphabet honors its letters as the building blocks of revealed books, divine names and attributes, and human speech and worship.
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p183/r1.anchor: وإنما أقسم الله بحروف المعجم، لشرفها وفضلها، ولأنها مباني كتبه المنزلة

IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p183/r4.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p183/r4.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p183/r4.claim: If the opening letters abbreviate divine attributes, this follows Arab shorthand: words replace related words, and letters replace others with nearby articulation, as in مدهته for مدحته and جدث/جدف.
IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p183/r4.anchor: وإن كان حروفا مأخوذة من صفات الله، فهذا فن من اختصار العرب

IBNHISHAM:v1p235#2/r3.author: Ibn Hishām
IBNHISHAM:v1p235#2/r3.speaker: عبيد
IBNHISHAM:v1p235#2/r3.claim: Ubayd's report says Muhammad annually secluded himself at Hira during Ramadan, fed the poor, and returned to circumambulate the Kaaba; Gabriel then came with a written silk cloth and commanded him to recite, repeating the embrace three times, after which Muhammad woke with the words fixed in his heart.
IBNHISHAM:v1p235#2/r3.anchor: قال عبيد: فكان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يجاور ذلك الشهر من كل سنة، يطعم من جاءه من المساكين

ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r1.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls the teaching of scientific benefits a supreme act of generosity: God teaches people what they did not know and moves them from ignorance to knowledge.
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r1.anchor: وليس وراء التكرم بإفادة الفوائد العلمية تكرم حيث قال : { الأكرم الذي علم بالقلم علم الإنسان ما لم يعلم }

ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r2.claim: He highlights writing as the finest knowledge because of its immense benefits.
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r2.anchor: ونبه على أفضل علم الكتابة لما فيه من المنافع العظيمة التي لا يحيط بها إلا هو

ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says writing preserves sciences, wisdom, ancient reports and writings, and revealed books; without it religious and worldly affairs could not be sustained.
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r3.anchor: وما دونت العلوم ، ولا قيدت الحكم ، ولا ضبطت أخبار الأولين ولا مقالاتهم ولا كتب الله المنزلة إلا بالكتابة

ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r4.claim: He says the very existence of writing and the pen suffices as evidence of God's precise wisdom and subtle governance.
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r4.anchor: ولو لم يكن على دقيق حكمة الله تعالى ولطيف تدبيره دليل إلا أمر الخط والقلم لكفى به

ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r5.speaker: بعضهم
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r5.claim: An unnamed poet likens pens to speckled snakes that move swiftly to the farthest reach, their black shafts moving only when white nibs play over them.
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r5.anchor: ولبعضهم في الأقلام : ورواقم رقش كمثل أراقم *** قطف الخطا نيالة أقصى المدى سود القوائم ما يجد مسيرها *** إلا إذا لعبت بها بيض المدى

ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r7.claim: The two objects of علم are omitted because the point is to attribute teaching to God.
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r7.anchor: ومفعولا علم محذوفان ، إذ المقصود إسناد التعليم إلى الله تعالى

ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r8.speaker: ابن الزبير
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r8.claim: A reading attributed to Ibn al-Zubayr supplies الخط after علّم; Abū Ḥayyān treats it as an explanatory gloss, not Qur'anic text, because it differs from the codex spelling.
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r8.anchor: وقدر بعضهم { الذي علم } الخط ، { بالقلم } : وهي قراءة تعزى لابن الزبير ، وهي عندي على سبيل التفسير

ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r9.claim: On the apparent reading, the one taught is every person who writes with a pen.
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r9.anchor: والظاهر أن المعلم كل من كتب بالقلم

ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r10.speaker: الضحاك
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r10.claim: Al-Dahhak identifies the person taught as Idris.

ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r11.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r11.claim: Another view identifies the person taught as Adam, the first to write.
ABUHAYYAN:96:4/r11.anchor: وقيل : آدم لأنه أول من كتب

ALUSI:96:4/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:4/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI:96:4/r1.claim: God taught what He taught through the pen without ulterior purpose; the unrestricted description as Most Generous is uniquely His, and the elative form intensifies the attribute.
ALUSI:96:4/r1.anchor: أي علم ما علم بواسطة القلم لا لغرض فهو صفة لا يشاركه تعالى في إطلاقها أحد فافعل للمبالغة

ALUSI:96:5/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r3.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:96:5/r3.claim: Some supply “writing” as the object of “taught” and attach “by the pen” to it.
ALUSI:96:5/r3.anchor: وقدر بعضهم مفعول علم الخط وجعل بالقلم متعلقاً به

ALUSI:96:5/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r4.speaker: ابن الزبير
ALUSI:96:5/r4.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr’s reading explicitly says “writing,” supporting the interpretation that writing is the object taught by means of the pen.
ALUSI:96:5/r4.anchor: وأيد بقراءة ابن الزبير الذي علم الخط بالقلم حيث صرح فيها بذلك

ALUSI:96:5/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r17.speaker: author
ALUSI:96:5/r17.claim: The one who taught by the pen is not identified in the verse.
ALUSI:96:5/r17.anchor: والظاهر أن المعلم بالقلم غير معين

ALUSI:96:5/r18.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r18.speaker: قيل
ALUSI:96:5/r18.claim: One view identifies the teacher by pen as every prophet who wrote.

ALUSI:96:5/r19.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r19.speaker: الضحاك
ALUSI:96:5/r19.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk identifies the teacher as Idrīs, to whom special alphabet inscriptions were also attributed; al-Ālūsī doubts these attributions.
ALUSI:96:5/r19.anchor: وقال الضحاك هو إدريس عليه السلام وهو من خط وقال كعب هو آدم عليه السلام وهو أول من كتب وقد نسبوا لآدم وإدريس عليهما السلام نقوشاً مخصوصة

ALUSI:96:5/r20.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r20.speaker: كعب
ALUSI:96:5/r20.claim: Kaʿb identifies the teacher as Adam and says he was the first to write; al-Ālūsī doubts the special scripts later attributed to Adam and Idrīs.
ALUSI:96:5/r20.anchor: وقال كعب هو آدم عليه السلام وهو أول من كتب وقد نسبوا لآدم وإدريس عليهما السلام نقوشاً مخصوصة في كتابة حروف الهجاء والذي يغلب على الظن عدم صحة ذلك

ALUSI:96:5/r21.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r21.speaker: author
ALUSI:96:5/r21.claim: The verse embeds praise of writing: its immense benefits and elevated ranks support religion and improve livelihood; pen and script alone would evidence divine wisdom.
ALUSI:96:5/r21.anchor: وقد أدمج سبحانه وتعالى التنبيه على فضل علم الكتابة لما فيه من المنافع العظيمة ونيل الرتب الفخيمة ولولاه لم يقم دين ولم يصلح عيش

ALUSI:96:5/r22.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r22.speaker: قيل
ALUSI:96:5/r22.claim: An unnamed poet praises writing with images of deadly serpent saliva and honey gathered by bees.
ALUSI:96:5/r22.anchor: لعاب الأفاعي القاتلات لعباه *** وأرى الجني

ALUSI:96:5/r23.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r23.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI:96:5/r23.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī attributes a couplet, perhaps to himself, that depicts pens as patterned serpents racing far and their black strokes moving over white blades.
ALUSI:96:5/r23.anchor: ومما نسبه الزمخشري في ذلك لبعضهم

ALUSI:96:5/r24.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r24.speaker: author
ALUSI:96:5/r24.claim: Writing was ancient among non-Arab peoples but comparatively recent among Arabs, especially in the Ḥijāz.
ALUSI:96:5/r24.anchor: وظاهر الآثار أن الكتابة في الأمم غير العرب قديمة

ALUSI:96:5/r25.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r25.speaker: غير واحد
ALUSI:96:5/r25.claim: Several authorities say writing reached the Arabs from al-Ḥīra, whose people had taken it from al-Anbār.
ALUSI:96:5/r25.anchor: وذكر غير واحد أن الكتابة نقلت إليهم من أهل الحيرة وأنهم أخذوها من أهل الأنبار

ALUSI:96:5/r26.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r26.speaker: الكلبي والهيثم بن عدي
ALUSI:96:5/r26.claim: Al-Kalbī and al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī say Ḥarb ibn Umayya brought Arabic script from al-ʿIrāq to Mecca via al-Ḥīra; the transmission is traced through Aslam ibn Asdara to its inventor Marāmir ibn Murra.
ALUSI:96:5/r26.anchor: وذكر الكلبي والهيثم بن عدي أن الناقل للخط العربي من العراق إلى الحجاز حرب بن أمية

ALUSI:96:5/r27.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r27.speaker: قيل
ALUSI:96:5/r27.claim: The Ḥimyarites had a disconnected script called musnad, regarded as prestigious and taught only to those authorized to learn it.
ALUSI:96:5/r27.anchor: وقيل كان لحمير كتابة يسمونها المسند منفصلة غير متصلة وكان لها شأن عندهم فلا يتعاطاها إلا من أذن له في تعلمها

ALUSI:96:5/r28.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:5/r28.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:96:5/r28.claim: Some classify the world’s writing systems into twelve roots; al-Ālūsī allows this if meant as origins, since their branches are nearly innumerable.
ALUSI:96:5/r28.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن جل كتابات الأمم اثنا عشر صنفاً العربية والحميرية والفارسية والعبرانية واليونانية والرومية والقبطية والبربرية والأندلسية والهندية والصينية والسريانية

ALUSI:96:8/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:96:8/r6.speaker: قيل
ALUSI:96:8/r6.claim: Some see these closing verses as embedding a warning against wealth, complementing the opening verses’ praise of knowledge and urging religion and learning over worldly life and riches.
ALUSI:96:8/r6.anchor: وفي هذه الآيات على ما قيل ادماج التنبيه على مذمة المال كما أن في الآيات الأول إدماج التنبيه على مدح العلم وكفى ذلك مرغباً في الدين والعلم ومنفراً عن الدنيا والمال

BAGHAWI:96:1/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:96:1/r2.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
BAGHAWI:96:1/r2.claim: Most commentators hold that this was the first sūra revealed and that the first revelation was its opening five verses, ending with “what he did not know.”
BAGHAWI:96:1/r2.anchor: أكثر المفسرين : على أن هذه السورة أول سورة نزلت من القرآن ، وأول ما نزل خمس آيات

BAGHAWI:96:1/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:96:1/r3.speaker: عائشة
BAGHAWI:96:1/r3.claim: Aisha recounts the Prophet’s true dreams, retreat and worship at Hira, then Gabriel’s command to read and three forceful embraces before reciting the opening revelation; Baghawi gives no grading.
BAGHAWI:96:1/r3.anchor: عن عائشة أم المؤمنين أنها قالت : " أول ما بدئ به رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من الوحي الرؤيا الصالحة

BAGHAWI:96:1/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:96:1/r4.speaker: عائشة
BAGHAWI:96:1/r4.claim: After the revelation the frightened Prophet returned to Khadija, who reassured him that God would never disgrace him because he maintained kinship, supported the needy, hosted guests, and aided people in hardship.
BAGHAWI:96:1/r4.anchor: فقالت خديجة : كلا ، والله ما يخزيك الله أبداً ، إنك لتصل الرحم ، وتحمل الكل ، وتكسب المعدوم

BAGHAWI:96:1/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:96:1/r6.speaker: الزهري
BAGHAWI:96:1/r6.claim: In a Bukhari version, al-Zuhri adds that revelation paused and the Prophet, in grief, repeatedly approached mountain peaks intending to throw himself down until Gabriel reassured him; the addition is introduced as “what reached us.”
BAGHAWI:96:1/r6.anchor: حتى حزن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فيما بلغنا حزناً غدا منه مراراً حتى يتردى من رؤوس شواهق الجبال

BAGHAWI:96:4/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:96:4/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:96:4/r1.claim: The pen is a means of writing and handwriting.
BAGHAWI:96:4/r1.anchor: الذي علم بالقلم } يعني الخط والكتابة

BAYDAWI:96:4/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:96:4/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:96:4/r1.claim: God taught writing by the pen, which preserves knowledge and conveys it to people far away.
BAYDAWI:96:4/r1.anchor: وقد قرئ به لتقيد به العلوم ويعلم به البعيد

BIQAI:96:4/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI:96:4/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI:96:4/r1.claim: God grants the illiterate Muslim community knowledge and gifts not granted to an earlier community, despite its members' shorter lifespans.
BIQAI:96:4/r1.anchor: يفيض على أمته الأمية من العلم والحظ ما لم يفضه على أمة قبلها

BIQAI:96:4/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI:96:4/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI:96:4/r2.claim: The teaching clause displays divine generosity: granting knowledge raises a human from a low rational state to a high, perfected one, warranting the description as most generous.
BIQAI:96:4/r2.anchor: مشعراً بوصفه سبحانه بالمنح بالعلم إلى ترتيب الحكم بالأكرمية

BIQAI:96:4/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI:96:4/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI:96:4/r3.claim: Teaching by the pen means teaching writing with it; this gift follows God's forbearance in not hastening punishment, out of generosity rather than fear of consequences or hope of gain.

DURR:96:1/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:96:1/r3.speaker: بعض علمائهم
DURR:96:1/r3.claim: Scholars heard by Muḥammad b. ʿAbbād said the opening through 96:5 was revealed at Ḥirāʾ; the sūra’s ending came later as God willed.
DURR:96:1/r3.anchor: عن ابن شهاب : حدثني محمد بن عباد بن جعفر المخزومي أنه سمع بعض علمائهم يقول

DURR:96:1/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:96:1/r6.speaker: عائشة
DURR:96:1/r6.claim: In ʿĀʾisha’s account, Gabriel commanded the unlettered Prophet to recite, squeezed him three times, then delivered the opening five verses at Ḥirāʾ.
DURR:96:1/r6.anchor: عن عائشة أم المؤمنين أنها قالت : «أول ما بدئ به رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من الوحي الرؤيا الصالحة

DURR:96:1/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:96:1/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR:96:1/r12.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the first revelation consisted of five verses, ending with “what he did not know.”
DURR:96:1/r12.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال : أول شيء أنزل من القرآن خمس آيات { اقرأ باسم ربك الذي خلق } إلى قوله : { ما لم يعلم } .

DURR:96:1/r15.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:96:1/r15.speaker: الزهري وعمرو بن دينار
DURR:96:1/r15.claim: Al-Zuhrī and ʿAmr b. Dīnār report that, at Ḥirāʾ, an angel brought the Prophet brocade bearing the opening five verses in writing.
DURR:96:1/r15.anchor: عن الزهري وعمرو بن دينار أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان بحراء إذا أتاه ملك بنمط من ديباج

DURR:96:1/r16.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:96:1/r16.speaker: عمرو بن جابر
DURR:96:1/r16.claim: ʿAmr b. Jābir likewise reports that an angel came to the Prophet at Ḥirāʾ with brocade inscribed through “what he did not know.”
DURR:96:1/r16.anchor: من طريق عمرو بن جابر أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان بحراء إذ أتاه ملك

DURR:96:1/r17.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:96:1/r17.speaker: عبد الله بن شداد
DURR:96:1/r17.claim: ʿAbd Allāh b. Shaddād recounts Gabriel’s repeated command to recite and squeezing of Muhammad, who then received the opening passage through 96:5.
DURR:96:1/r17.anchor: عن عبد الله بن شداد قال : «أتى جبريل محمداً صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال : يا محمد اقرأ

DURR:96:1/r19.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:96:1/r19.speaker: عائشة
DURR:96:1/r19.claim: A second ʿĀʾisha account describes Gabriel’s vast appearance, washing the Prophet’s opened chest, teaching the opening five verses, and weighing him against men; Michael says his community will follow.
DURR:96:1/r19.anchor: عن عائشة «أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم اعتكف هو وخديجة شهراً فوافق ذلك رمضان

DURR:96:4/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:96:4/r1.speaker: قتادة
DURR:96:4/r1.claim: Qatāda calls the pen a great divine blessing: without it religion would not be upheld and life would not be set right.
DURR:96:4/r1.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله : { الذي علم بالقلم } قال : القلم نعمة من الله عظيمة

DURR:96:5/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:96:5/r1.speaker: قتادة
DURR:96:5/r1.claim: Qatāda calls the pen a great divine blessing: without it religion would not be upheld and life would not be set right.
DURR:96:5/r1.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله : { الذي علم بالقلم } قال : القلم نعمة من الله عظيمة

IBNASHUR:96:1/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:96:1/r7.speaker: عائشة، أبو موسى الأشعري
IBNASHUR:96:1/r7.claim: Sound reports from Aisha establish that these first five verses were first, delivered to Muhammad in Hira on Ramadan 17, year 40 after the Elephant; Abu Musa and most exegetes agree.
IBNASHUR:96:1/r7.anchor: وهي أول سورة نزلت في القرآن كما ثبت في الأحاديث الصحيحة الواضحة ، ونزل أولها بغار حراء على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

IBNASHUR:96:1/r17.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:96:1/r17.speaker: عائشة
IBNASHUR:96:1/r17.claim: Aisha's report is Ibn Ashur's basis for identifying these five verses as the first revelation to Muhammad in Hira.
IBNASHUR:96:1/r17.anchor: هذا أول ما أوحي به من القرآن إلى محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم لما ثبت عن عائشة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

IBNASHUR:96:4/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:96:4/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:96:4/r1.claim: A qalam is a piece of reed trimmed smooth and slit lengthwise at its tip; when dipped in ink it writes on paper and similar surfaces. Ibn Ashur refers to 3:44.
IBNASHUR:96:4/r1.anchor: والقلم : شَظيَّة من قصب ترقق وتثقّف وتبرى بالسكينِ لتكون ملساء بين الأصابع

IBNASHUR:96:5/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:96:5/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:96:5/r3.claim: The two teachings point to three routes of knowledge: written records and reading books, oral instruction and dictation, and discoveries or inventions produced by reasoning; writing lets learning pass across distance and generations.
IBNASHUR:96:5/r3.anchor: وقد حصلتْ من ذكر التعليم بالقلم والتعليم الأعم إشارة إلى ما يتلقاه الإنسان من التعاليم سواء كان بالدرس أم بمطالعة الكتب

IBNASHUR:96:5/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:96:5/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:96:5/r6.claim: The verses signal God's concern that the revealed Qur'an be written down; Muhammad therefore appointed scribes for revelation from the beginning of his mission.
IBNASHUR:96:5/r6.anchor: وفي الآية إشارة إلى الاهتمام بعلم الكتابة وبأن الله يريد أن يُكتَب للنبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم ما ينزل عليه من القرآن

IBNASHUR:96:5/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:96:5/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:96:5/r7.claim: The command to read followed by teaching through the pen hints that Muhammad remained unlettered, a feature completing the Qur'an's miraculous character, as 29:48 says.
IBNASHUR:96:5/r7.anchor: وفي الاقتصار على أمر الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم بالقراءة ثم إخباره بأن الله علّم الإنسان بالقلم إيماء إلى استمرار صفة الأمية

IBNASHUR:96:5/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:96:5/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:96:5/r8.claim: These are the final verses of the five that were first revealed to Muhammad in the cave of Hira.
IBNASHUR:96:5/r8.anchor: وهذه آخر الخمس الآيات التي هي أول ما أنزل على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في غار حراء

IBNATIYYA:96:4/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:96:4/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:96:4/r1.claim: Writing with the pen is a divine blessing and a sign, with great benefit for communication and preserving knowledge.
IBNATIYYA:96:4/r1.anchor: ثم عدد تعالى نعمة الكتاب { بالقلم } على الناس ،   وهي موضع عبرة وأعظم منفعة في المخاطبات

IBNKATHIR:96:1/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r2.speaker: عائشة
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r2.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that true dreams began revelation, then the Prophet loved solitude, worshiped at Ḥirāʾ for several nights, and Khadīja supplied his provisions.
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r2.anchor: عن عائشة قالت : أول ما بدئ به رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من الوحي الرؤيا الصادقة في النوم

IBNKATHIR:96:1/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r3.speaker: عائشة
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r3.claim: ʿĀʾisha recounts Gabriel's three forceful embraces in the cave, Muhammad's repeated reply that he could not read, and Gabriel's recitation of the opening revelation; Muhammad returned trembling.
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r3.anchor: فجاءه الملك فيه فقال : اقرأ . قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

IBNKATHIR:96:1/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r4.speaker: خديجة
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r4.claim: In ʿĀʾisha's report, Khadīja reassures Muhammad that God will never disgrace him, citing his kinship ties, truthfulness, bearing burdens, hospitality, and help in adversity.
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r4.anchor: يا خديجة ، ما لي : فأخبرها الخبر وقال : " قد خشيت علي " . فقالت له : كلا أبشر فوالله لا يخزيك الله أبدا ؛ إنك لتصل الرحم

IBNKATHIR:96:1/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r5.speaker: ورقة بن نوفل
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r5.claim: Waraqa ibn Nawfal, Khadīja's relative, was a pre-Islamic Christian who wrote Arabic and Gospel material in it; he identified the angel as the messenger sent to Moses, predicted opposition and expulsion, and promised support if alive.
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r5.anchor: فقال ورقة : هذا الناموس الذي أنزل على موسى

IBNKATHIR:96:1/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r6.claim: Ibn Kathīr adds, with the qualifier “as has reached us,” that after Waraqa's death revelation paused and grief brought Muhammad repeatedly to mountain peaks, where Gabriel reassured him he was truly God's messenger.
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r6.anchor: وفَتَر الوحي فترة حتى حَزن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم - فيما بلغنا -

IBNKATHIR:96:1/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r7.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r7.claim: Ibn Kathīr says the report is transmitted in both Ṣaḥīḥs through al-Zuhrī; he notes that he examined its chain, text, and meanings in his Bukhārī commentary.
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r7.anchor: وهذا الحديث مخرج في الصحيحين من حديث الزهري

IBNKATHIR:96:1/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r8.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r8.claim: Ibn Kathīr says these opening verses are God's first mercy to humanity and His first blessing upon them.
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r8.anchor: وهُنَّ أول رحمة رَحم الله بها العباد

IBNKATHIR:96:1/r11.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r11.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r11.claim: Knowledge occurs mentally, orally, and in writing; written knowledge entails both mental and oral forms, while neither mental nor oral knowledge necessarily entails writing.

IBNKATHIR:96:1/r12.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r12.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:96:1/r12.claim: An unnamed athar urges people to preserve knowledge by writing it down.
